extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and observers of Russian law, media freedom and censorship
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the 2022–2023 Russian federal laws criminalizing 'discrediting' and dissemination of 'unreliable information' about state bodies and the armed forces, their amendments, enforcement practice, penalties, and effects on media and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrediting the Russian Armed Forces (article 20.3.3; article 280.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'discrediting' of the armed forces, including calls that their use was not in the interests of the Russian Federation, is prohibited: administrative fines under article 20.3.3 and criminal liability under article 280.3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page wording: 'A "discrediting" of the armed forces, including calls that their use was not in the interests of the Russian Federation, carried large fines for natural and juridicial persons (article 20.3.3) and up to five years imprisonment (article 280.3).' Later amendments (March 2023) increased maximum prison terms for 'discrediting' to up to seven years. Examples of prosecution under this standard (speeches, social-media posts, remarks at concerts, council meetings) are given throughout the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissemination of 'unreliable information' about the armed forces (article 207.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissemination of 'unreliable information' about the armed forces and its operation is criminalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial formulation in the article: 'The dissemination of "unreliable information" about the armed forces and its operation could be punished with up to fifteen years imprisonment (article 207.3).' The article also notes a later amendment (March 2023) changed maximum terms (cited as up to seven years for discrediting or disseminating unreliable information); the text emphasises that dissemination of 'unreliable information' is treated as a criminal offence (an exception to the administrative-first approach). Examples given include prosecution for reporting on alleged military-caused civilian deaths (Bucha, Mariupol) and other war reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calls to impose sanctions (article 20.3.4; article 284.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls to impose sanctions against Russia, Russian citizens or Russian legal entities are prohibited and punishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article: 'Calls to impose sanctions against Russia, Russian citizens or Russian legal entities carried a large fine (article 20.3.4) and up to 3 years imprisonment (article 284.2).' It also notes later amendments increased maximum imprisonment for calling for sanctions (cited as up to five years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dadin scheme of enforcement (administrative first, criminal for repeat offences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement follows the so‑called 'Dadin scheme': a first offence is punished administratively by fines with subsequent offences punished under the criminal code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasises the administrative-then-criminal escalation and notes an exception: dissemination of 'unreliable information' about the armed forces is only punishable under the criminal code (i.e., not subject to first-offence administrative-only treatment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating internet publications as continuing violations; retroactive prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations committed through Internet publications are considered continuing violations, enabling prosecution for material published before the laws came into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prevailing approach in Russian law-enforcement 'considers any violations committed through Internet publications as continuing violations; this allows authorities to persecute people for material published before the laws came into effect. The statute of limitations is taken from the time when violating material is removed from the Internet.' This is cited as a practice enabling retroactive enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrajurisdictional extension to other state bodies (25 March 2022 amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments expanded punishments for discrediting or disseminating unreliable information regarding the extraterritorial exercise of powers by other Russian state bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article: on 25 March 2022, federal laws No.62-FZ and No.63-FZ amended articles 20.3.3 and 207.3 to extend punishments to extraterritorial actions of bodies including the National Guard, FSB, Ministry of Emergency Situations, General Prosecutor's Office, Investigative Committee, and Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to volunteers, formations and mercenaries (18 March 2023 amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments extended punishments for discrediting or disseminating unreliable information to the activities of volunteers, their formations and organizations aimed at assisting the tasks of the armed forces (including mercenaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article: federal laws No.57-FZ and No.58-FZ (18 March 2023) made additional amendments extending the laws' scope to volunteers and mercenaries such as Wagner Group. The article notes this is notable because mercenarism is otherwise prohibited under Russia's criminal code. The amendments also increased maximum prison terms (e.g., up to seven years for discrediting or disseminating unreliable information and up to five years for calling for sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations and sanctions for platforms, publishers and online services (Roskomnadzor actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory measures include demands to remove 'unreliable socially significant materials', fines, blocking threats and orders for search engines to mark violator sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roskomnadzor threatened to block Wikipedia over articles about the invasion; sent requests to remove five specific Russian Wikipedia articles; a court fined the Wikimedia Foundation 3 million rubles for failing to remove seven Wikipedia articles; authorities ordered search engines to mark Wikipedia as a violator of Russian laws. The legal standard cited in regulator requests is failure to remove 'unreliable socially significant materials, as well as other prohibited information.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and sanctions regime (fines, imprisonment, and corporate liability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws provide a mix of administrative fines and criminal penalties (including multi‑year imprisonment) and apply to both natural persons and juridical persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific penalties cited: large fines under administrative articles (20.3.3, 20.3.4), imprisonment up to specified terms under criminal articles (207.3, 280.3, 284.2); the article lists historic and amended maximum sentences and numerous individual sentences and fines as examples (ranging from fines to multi‑year prison terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad and vague definitions enabling wide interpretation ('discrediting' and 'unreliable information')
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory terms 'discrediting' and 'unreliable information' are used in broad and context‑dependent ways, enabling wide prosecutorial interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article illustrates vagueness with descriptions and examples (e.g., prosecuting statements that 'didn't refer to the Russian Armed Forces' yet were judged as discrediting, prosecutions for social-media posts, comments on events such as Bucha and Mariupol). It notes criticism from human rights groups and that the laws 'are part of Russia’s ruthless effort to suppress all dissent' (Human Rights Watch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective enforcement / 'perversion of law' (political/exemptions in practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice the laws have been applied inconsistently: political opponents, independent journalists and critics are targeted while some ultra‑nationalists and pro‑war activists avoid prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article labels this phenomenon 'perversion of law' and gives examples: Kremlin‑favoured political scientists and pro‑war figures using 'war' without consequences, while opposition figures were prosecuted; high‑profile prosecutions and high sentence variability are documented to illustrate selective enforcement.
